reply.text:
This means Git tried to combine two branches that have **no commit in common**, so it has no base to merge from. Git blocks this by default because it usually signals a mistake.

The most common cause is a local repo that was started separately from the remote one. For example, you ran `git init`, made some commits, and added a remote on GitHub that already had its own commits (such as an auto-generated README or LICENSE). Each side has a complete history, but the two histories never meet.

To see what you're dealing with, check both histories:

```
git log --oneline              # your local history
git log --oneline origin/main  # the remote's history (after git fetch)
git remote -v                  # confirm you're pointing at the right remote
```

Then pick a fix:

- **Both sides are the same project, and you want to keep both histories:**
  ```
  git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories
  ```
  You'll probably get merge conflicts on files that exist on both sides, such as the README. Resolve them, then commit.

- **The remote is empty or junk and your local history should win:** you can force-push your local branch, but this overwrites the remote, so only do it if you're sure nothing there matters.

- **You cloned or pulled the wrong repo:** fix the remote URL with `git remote set-url origin <correct-url>` instead of merging.

If you paste the output of the commands above, I can tell you which case applies.
